topics.title: Selling a Nervos DAO withdrawal: CKB now, no new script

recent_posts.topic_title: Selling a Nervos DAO withdrawal: CKB now, no new script
recent_posts.author: LusoCryptoLabs
recent_posts.content_text:
A Nervos DAO deposit pays out at the end of the 180-epoch cycle in which its withdrawal request lands, with cycles counted from the deposit. Someone who needs their CKB early waits up to about 30 days. iCKB solves this for CKB deposited through iCKB, but an existing deposit cannot move into it.
We want to build a third option in the Cellula wallet: sell the withdrawal. The depositor gets CKB now, and the buyer claims the deposit when it matures. Before we build it, we would like to hear where this breaks.
How it works
Withdrawal phase 1 turns a deposit cell into a withdrawing cell. The DAO script lets that withdrawing cell use any lock (dao.c v0.5.4 L332-L334). Since 2023, nodes require it to have a lock of the same serialized size as the deposit’s, for deposits included at or after block 10,000,000 (RFC 0023, DaoScriptSizeVerifier). phroi found the issue that led to that rule.
So one transaction can:
spend the seller’s deposit cell and create the withdrawing cell under the buyer’s lock, at the same index;
spend the buyer’s CKB and pay the seller.
Both sign the same transaction. No new on-chain script is needed.
flow1960×618 56.9 KB
On testnet, both sides on secp256k1 locks: the buyer paid 995.89 CKB for a 1,000 CKB claim with a full cycle (about 30 days) left, about 5% a year (0xb376a515). The deposit was made 3 blocks earlier. A lock of another size is refused by the node: “The lock script size of deposit cell at index 0 does not match the withdrawing cell at the same index”.
Cellula wallet accounts can do it today with the wallet’s own lock, also on testnet: a full account sold a 300 CKB claim to another full account (0x85cf8e0c), and a starter address to another starter address (0x6bdaf749). The wallet app has no code for this yet.
The buyer’s claim, on a local dev chain with the same DAO binary as mainnet (ckb 0.210.0, 10-block epochs): after maturity the buyer got exactly the same compensation as a normal withdrawal from the same blocks. A claim one epoch early, and the seller trying to spend the cell, were both refused. The testnet claims above mature around 2026-12-04.
Price
At maturity the buyer receives the deposit plus the compensation up to the phase 1 block. The claim earns nothing after phase 1: dao.c takes the rate from the withdrawing cell’s own block. So:
the yield earned so far goes to the buyer on chain, and the price pays it back to the seller;
the yield for the days left is given up;
the discount is what the buyer earns for waiting.
Example: a 10,000 CKB deposit made 10 days ago is worth about 10,006 CKB at maturity, 20 days from now. A buyer who wants 5% a year pays about 9,979 CKB now and earns 27 CKB. Waiting the full cycle would have paid the seller about 10,017 CKB. The wallet would show both numbers.
How much it would be used
We measured mainnet withdrawals over the 158 days to 2026-11-04: 896 phase 1 withdrawals, 838.7M CKB. This leaves out the iCKB pool and a dCKB drain in August, the 205 cells whose lock changed at phase 1. Time from phase 1 to maturity:

About half (49% of withdrawals, 41% of the CKB) were within 3 days of maturity. About a third were more than a week away. So this is a small feature for people who need their CKB quickly, not a large market.
Credit and earlier objections
tianlitao proposed this in t/8956#7 (English in #8), as an extension of the instant convert service xxuejie described in #1. phroi answered that it is “not really viable” and listed the problems (#11, #15). Our answers:
Unbounded liquidity, a DoS with a huge deposit. Each quote is for one deposit, and each buyer sets the largest deposit it will take. A deposit nobody buys waits for its cycle, as today.
“What if the user deposited 4 years ago, is he not entitled to a part of his yield?” He keeps it: the yield earned so far is part of the price.
Deposits are NFTs, the user must choose one. The wallet shows each deposit with its time left and its price, and the user picks.
Same index for deposit and withdrawal, at most 64 outputs. One deposit per transaction, built by the wallet.
iCKB, and dCKB before it, already change the lock at phase 1 inside their own protocols. We found no service that buys single claims from users.
Traps and limits
Who signs last. Any spend of a deposit is a phase 1, so the seller cannot cancel cheaply, and a buyer holding a half-signed transaction could wait while the claim grows. So the buyer signs first and the seller signs last.
Cycle boundary. A signed transaction stays valid after the boundary (since is only a lower bound). If phase 1 lands after it, the claim moves to the next cycle, about 30 more days. So each quote has a deadline a few epochs before the boundary, and at the deadline the buyer spends, on chain, the input reserved for that quote, which voids it. Replace-by-fee is not enough: on a dev chain it replaced a sale that was pending or just proposed, but once the sale could be committed, the next block committed it anyway.
Quote spam. Each signed quote ties up one of the buyer’s cells, so a buyer limits open quotes per requester.
Lock sizes. A buyer needs a lock of the seller’s size, and one key can back several. Common sizes: 73 bytes (secp256k1, and multisig or ACP with 20-byte args), 75 (JoyID, Omnilock with 22-byte args, ACP with 22). Cellula wallet accounts are 75 bytes (starter addresses, the size of JoyID) or 85 bytes (full accounts, which sell to another full account). The buyer’s lock must also handle phase 2, which needs an absolute-epoch since.
What the buyer checks. The DAO type, all-zero deposit data, the output lock and the deposit block. dao.c checks the headers, so the seller cannot fake the claim.
No resale. A claim changes hands once: a withdrawing cell can only be spent in phase 2, after maturity. If the buyer loses its key, the claim is lost.
Fees and minimums. The buyer pays the fee. The payment to the seller is a normal cell: at least 61 CKB on secp256k1, a little more on bigger locks.
A rule that may change. The node’s code calls the lock-size check “a temporary solution till Nervos DAO script can be properly upgraded”. A future DAO script could forbid a new lock at phase 1, and this would stop working.
Voting. chenyukang’s ckb-treasury-lab#15 notes that withdrawing cells count as voting weight. We added there that a sale moves them, and supported counting deposits only.
Plan
In the Cellula wallet, on testnet first: for each deposit, “CKB now” next to the value at maturity.
Open offers: public, in an open format any wallet can read, so any buyer can answer, the iCKB bot included.
No fee for us. The wallet only builds the transaction both sides sign. We do not buy claims, hold anyone’s CKB or take a side.
No funding is asked here. Does anyone see a flaw, or would you make offers?

recent_posts.topic_title: Selling a Nervos DAO withdrawal: CKB now, no new script
recent_posts.author: Code3ks
recent_posts.content_text:
Interesting approach. I like that this creates an option for existing DAO depositors to access liquidity without introducing a new script or requiring them to migrate into iCKB.
One question worth exploring is how the open-offer mechanism handles price discovery and buyer protection, especially around the cycle boundary where a transaction could push the claim into another 30-day cycle. Could a standardized quote format with clear expiry conditions help reduce that risk?
I think this could be a useful addition to the CKB ecosystem, particularly if different wallets and liquidity providers can participate without relying on a single intermediary.

recent_posts.topic_title: Selling a Nervos DAO withdrawal: CKB now, no new script
recent_posts.author: LusoCryptoLabs
recent_posts.content_html:
Thanks, that is the plan, and we tested the cancel path before answering.

Price discovery. Quotes would be per deposit. The wallet would send the deposit’s out point to several buyers, each would answer with a price, and the wallet would show the best one next to the value at maturity. Quotes would be public, so anyone can compare them.

Buyer protection at the boundary. A CKB transaction has no expiry (since is only a lower bound), so the buyer has to enforce the deadline, not the chain. A quote would carry:

  • the deposit out point and the claim epoch it assumes;
  • the price and the seller’s payment lock;
  • valid_until, a few epochs before the cycle boundary;
  • the buyer’s signature, over a transaction that uses an input cell kept for that quote only.

At valid_until, if the sale is not on chain, the buyer spends that input on chain, which voids the quote. Our wallet would also refuse to send a sale after valid_until. The seller signs last, so a buyer cannot sit on a half-signed deal, and the buyer’s signature binds the price.

Tested on a local dev chain (ckb 0.210.0):

  • buyer first and seller last works without re-signing; a seller who changes the price after the buyer signed is refused;
  • a sale sent after the buyer spent its input is refused (TransactionFailedToResolve), and the deposit stays a deposit and can be quoted again;
  • replace-by-fee is not a safe cancel: it replaced a sale that was pending or just proposed, but once the sale could be committed, the next block committed it anyway, 4 times out of 4. We corrected that line in the post.

Standard format. That is what we mean by open offers. We would write a short spec next to the wallet code, so other wallets and liquidity providers can quote or accept without anyone in the middle.

recent_posts.topic_title: Selling a Nervos DAO withdrawal: CKB now, no new script
recent_posts.author: LusoCryptoLabs
recent_posts.content_text:
Thanks @phroi,
Agreed on both. A sold claim is not composable, and a buyer has to take the whole deposit, since deposits cannot be split. That is why each buyer sets the largest deposit it will take, and why we called it a small feature.
On buying and selling deposits without withdrawing, do you mean deposits made under a lock whose control can move, like a proxy lock owned by another cell? That keeps the yield and allows resale, but only for deposits made that way from the start. This sale is for deposits that already sit under a plain lock.
That route also matters for voting, it lets a deposit’s weight change hands without a withdrawal, so I added a note to ckb-treasury-lab#15.

recent_posts.author: LusoCryptoLabs
recent_posts.content_text:
Thanks @phroi, and for pointing xjd and chenyukang at the note.
Agreed: no lock rule stops a custodian, or a market off chain, from renting votes. Deposit-only removes the cheapest route, the one that needs no trust: a claim bought and paid for in a single transaction.
What the weight should be is a bigger question than this thread. Ward only proves who controls a lock, so it works the same whether a platform weighs deposits, people or reputation. The binding side is here: t/11130 Let any wallet bind its Nervos DAO deposit on Metaforo .

topics.title: Let any wallet bind its Nervos DAO deposit on Metaforo

recent_posts.topic_title: Let any wallet bind its Nervos DAO deposit on Metaforo
recent_posts.author: LusoCryptoLabs
recent_posts.content_text:
A note first: we have a proposal in the discussion stage (t/11089). This post is separate and long term. Nothing here needs to happen before or during that vote, and it is fine to look at it afterwards. Whether our proposal passes or not, we will keep working on this.
The problem
To vote, Metaforo binds a Nervos DAO address through a Neuron-style message signature. In Metaforo’s web app the bind call sends only the message and the signature, and the server answers with a default single-key address. So only deposits under that lock can carry voting weight.
What we found, read from the public Metaforo data and the explorer on 2026-11-04:
Across the 176 voters of the 38 polls we read, all 612 bound addresses use the default secp256k1 lock.
Metaforo already lets people sign in with JoyID, but the deposits at the JoyID address are not counted. Four voters who sign in with JoyID hold 13,421,200 CKB in Nervos DAO at their JoyID addresses. One of them voted three times with 101,000 CKB, the deposit at their bound Neuron address, while 600,200 CKB sat in the DAO at their JoyID address.
Omnilock, multisig and smart contract wallets cannot bind at all.
@janx asked for this in 2024 (t/7803#2): “Can we make NervosDAO deposit binding and voting accessible to JoyID/Neuron/… users?”
Two changes, from the smallest
Count the Nervos DAO deposits at the JoyID address a voter signs in with. Metaforo already knows that address.
Accept a lock proof as a second way to bind. With it, any wallet can prove it controls the lock of a deposit.
For the second, we wrote Ward, an open spec and verifier (MIT). It is the CKB counterpart of Ethereum’s EIP-1271 and Bitcoin’s BIP-322:
the platform issues a message (domain, account, lock hash, chain, time, nonce);
the wallet signs a proof transaction that commits to it and can never land on chain, because its input does not exist;
the platform runs the lock’s own code on that transaction, with its cell deps read live from the chain, and accepts if the lock does.
Tested on testnet, each with controls that must fail: the default lock, multisig 2-of-3, anyone-can-pay, Omnilock (Doge auth), a Nostr lock, JoyID (signed in the JoyID app) and the Cellula smart account. Not covered yet: JoyID sub-keys and mainnet. An adversarial review found two problems in the first version, a capped key binding a whole account and one lock bound to many accounts; both are fixed and tested, and the spec lists the rules a platform must keep, such as one binding per lock and no rebinding during a vote.
The weight rule stays as it is: current Nervos DAO deposits at bound addresses. Portal Wallet support was added in 2023 the same way, as a change in Metaforo (t/7053), so we think this does not need a meta-rule vote. Please correct us if it does.
What we offer
Help with the integration, and the verifier as it is, MIT.
If useful, we host a verifier endpoint at no cost.
No funding is asked. @terrytai, as the owner of the CKB group on Metaforo, and @zz_tovarishch, could you tell us the right way to take this to the Metaforo team?

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program Proposal: Corven cloud-native IDE
recent_posts.author: xingtianchunyan
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @lestonEth (Jimleston),
I’m glad to share that the Spark Program Committee has approved your Corven proposal for a grant of 520 USD.
The committee recognizes the project’s value in lowering the barrier to entry for CKB and Fiber Network development. The revised budget and approval-dependent timeline are also noted, and the committee appreciates the effort to keep costs focused on the essential logistics for the two physical sessions.

recent_posts.topic_title: A Revenue Layer for CKB Nodes
recent_posts.author: psawyerberlin
recent_posts.content_text:
Update, November 2026: CKB Service Runner is live, and so is its new home
When I started this thread, the question was: what if CKB nodes could become a revenue-generating opportunity? Six weeks later there is running code, a public monitor and the first nodes on mainnet.
CSR Network Monitor
What exists today
CKB Service Runner (CSR) is an optional program that runs beside your CKB full node. It is not part of ckb and changes nothing in the protocol.
A dashboard for your node. Sync state, tip, peers, CPU, RAM and disk on one page at 127.0.0.1, never exposed to the internet. Free, no CKB needed.
Proof that it is a real full node. CSR proves the node’s identity with the node’s own P2P key. The CSR Network Monitor sends each runner a signed challenge every 10 minutes (tip and block hashes) and fetches blocks over P2P once a day.
A public ranking. Availability over 30 and 365 days, sync, age and network diversity. Joining the ranking needs no registration and no stake.
Linux and Windows. Linux: one installer from GitHub, signed self-updates. Windows (beta): download the zip, double-click install.cmd. It works with ckb.exe or with Neuron’s internal mainnet full node.
Mainnet vs. testnet
Mainnet
Testnet
Node dashboard
Monitor checks and ranking
Service Runtime (paid jobs)
opens at the gate
running now
On testnet the whole loop already works: jobs arrive, the runner executes them, settles on chain and collects tips. My own testnet runner has settled 31 jobs so far.
The gate: 20 seats
The mainnet Service Runtime opens when the network is ready for it, not before:
20 ranked runners
120 days of monitor history
no single ASN above 25 **, no single **country above 50
The landing page shows these 20 seats live, and you can watch them fill up. Every node that joins now takes one of them.
(I lowered the target on 31 Oct from 12 months / 60 nodes. A gate nobody can reach protects nothing, and these limits still keep any one provider or country from dominating.)
What it costs
Dashboard and ranking: nothing.
Running paid jobs (later on mainnet, now on testnet): a Nervos DAO deposit of at least 10,000 CKB, which stays yours and keeps earning DAO interest, plus about 700 CKB in the runner wallet for its registry cell and fees. Only fees are spent. Everything else comes back.
What runners will earn from
Useful services for CKB dApps that need an always-on, independent party: monitoring events, sending alerts, running oracles, automatically pushing due transactions and more. The first consumers in the design are CRT (a threshold-secret service) and an optional CSR integration for crowdfunding campaigns.
How you can help
Node operators: install CSR and take a seat. Even as a dashboard only, every ranked node brings the gate closer.
Windows: one-click download (latest), then follow the 4 steps on the landing page
Linux: install guide on GitHub
Testers: run a testnet node with the Service Runtime on. I will sponsor the testnet stake for the first testers. Ask in Telegram.
dApp builders: which jobs would you hand to independent full nodes? Reply here. That decides what gets built next.
Everyone: critique the design. The monitor is a reputation source, not a proof, and trust-minimised rather than trustless. Point out where that is not enough.
Links
Landing page and monitor: CSR Network Monitor (testnet)
Runner source and releases: GitHub - ckb-service-runner/ckb-service-runner: Side application for CKB full nodes: dashboard, node ranking, and a sandboxed service runtime · GitHub
Monitor source: GitHub - ckb-service-runner/csr-network-monitor: CSR Network Monitor — probes CKB Service Runners, publishes availability, ranking and a weekly on-chain stat cell · GitHub
Telegram (install help, release news): Telegram: View @ckbrunner
Thanks to everyone who commented so far, and to the first operator besides me who already put a node on the map.
